findings.situation: A filer's solar system was installed in 2024 on a newly built home they first moved into in 2025, so the cost counts in 2025, but the help tells them it counts only in the year installation was completed.
findings.source_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins" (also reconstruction: "when your original use of the reconstructed home begins")
findings.why: The help states only the completed-installation timing rule. It leaves out the new-construction and reconstruction rule, so these 2025 costs would be left off line 1.

findings.situation: A filer completes installation in 2025 on a home under construction that they do not begin using until 2026, and enters the cost under the help's rule even though it belongs to a later year.
findings.source_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"; help: "A cost counts in 2025 when the original installation is completed."
findings.why: Under the help's timing rule, construction-related costs that are treated as paid in another year get pulled into 2025.

findings.situation: A filer uses the solar property 40% for business (for example, a home office or business use of part of the home) and enters the full cost.
findings.source_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "If less than 80% of the use of an item is for nonbusiness purposes, only that portion of the costs that is allocable to the nonbusiness use can be used to determine either credit."
findings.why: Neither the question nor the help mentions the business-use allocation, so a truthful filer reports the gross cost instead of the nonbusiness portion.

findings.situation: A filer installs solar panels on a rental house or other property they own in the U.S. but never lived in, and includes that cost because the question says the home 'need not be your main home.'
findings.source_text: i5695 p. 1, Home: "A home is where you lived in 2025"; p. 2: "more than one home that you used as a residence during 2025"; question: "for a home in the United States (it need not be your main home)"
findings.why: The question never requires that the filer lived in or used the home as a residence. An ordinary reader would count any dwelling they own, including properties the credit does not cover.

findings.why: The question can be read as ranking doors by gross price and then entering that door's net cost, or as entering the highest net cost. Because 19c caps each door separately at $250 and the next doors go to 19d, the two readings give different 19a amounts and can change the credit.

findings.situation: A filer's newly built home had its wind turbine installed in 2024, and the filer first moved in during 2025; the filer answers zero because the installation was completed in 2024.
findings.source_text: i5695 p. 1, Costs: "For purposes of the residential clean energy credit only, costs connected with the construction of a home are treated as being paid when your original use of the constructed home begins"; for reconstruction, costs are paid "when your original use of the reconstructed home begins"
findings.why: The help gives only the installation-completed timing rule. It leaves out the construction and reconstruction rule, under which these costs count in 2025, the year the filer's original use begins. A truthful answer therefore omits them. In the reverse case (installed in 2025, moved in during 2026), the filer would wrongly include them.

findings.situation: A filer installs a small wind turbine at a home where 30% of the use is business use, for example a home-based business, and enters the full cost.

findings.why: The question and help never mention limiting the cost to the nonbusiness portion. A truthful answer brings in the business-use share, which line 6a must not include.

findings.situation: A filer installs a wind turbine on a U.S. rental property or other house the filer never lived in during 2025 and includes the cost because the question says the home 'need not be your main home'.

findings.why: The question allows any U.S. home that is not the main home but does not say the filer must have lived there. A truthful answer can therefore include property at a dwelling the filer did not use as a residence.
